key_terms.meaning: Pump in which the impeller pushes water mainly along the shaft axis; gives high discharge at low head.
Pump in which water leaves the impeller partly radially and partly axially; between centrifugal and axial types.
Vertical multistage centrifugal pump lowered into a borewell to lift water from a deep water table.
Rotary positive-displacement pump in which two meshing gears trap liquid and push it to the delivery side.
Manually operated reciprocating pump, common in villages, that lifts water by piston strokes.
Pump with no moving parts in the well; a high-velocity water jet entrains and lifts the water.
Positive-displacement pump in which a piston or plunger sucks a fixed volume and pushes it out each stroke.
Positive-displacement pump using rotating gears, vanes, lobes or screws to trap and move liquid.
Rotary pump with sliding vanes in a rotor; liquid is trapped between vanes and casing and carried to delivery.
Pump that traps a fixed volume of liquid per cycle and forces it out; flow is almost independent of head.
The outlet pipe, valves and fittings that carry water from the pump to its destination.
Rotodynamic pump in which a spinning impeller throws water outward and the casing converts velocity into pressure.
Spiral casing of gradually increasing area around the impeller; it slows the water and raises its pressure.
Head measured between pump suction and delivery gauges; the useful head developed by the pump, in metres of water.
Lowest impeller speed at which the head generated by centrifugal action equals the manometric head, so pumping can begin.
Net positive suction head: absolute pressure head at pump inlet minus vapour pressure head; the margin against cavitation, in metres.
Formation and sudden collapse of vapour bubbles in low-pressure regions, causing noise, vibration and metal erosion.
Graph of pump head, power or efficiency against discharge at constant speed.
Ideal discharge minus actual discharge of a reciprocating pump, usually expressed as a percentage of ideal discharge.
Closed air chamber fitted on the suction or delivery pipe of a reciprocating pump to smooth flow and reduce friction work.

takeaways: Pumps add energy to water; rotodynamic pumps use a spinning impeller, while positive-displacement pumps trap and push fixed volumes.
A centrifugal pump first creates velocity head in the impeller and then converts most of it into pressure head in the volute or diffuser.
Manometric head is less than the head produced by the impeller because hydraulic, mechanical and volumetric losses consume part of the input.
A centrifugal pump starts lifting water only when the impeller head exceeds the manometric head; this condition fixes the minimum starting speed.
Pumps in series add their heads at the same discharge; pumps in parallel add their discharges at the same head.
Cavitation begins when local pressure falls to vapour pressure; NPSH is the safety margin, and reducing suction lift helps protect the pump.
Performance curves show that head falls and power usually rises as discharge increases; the duty point is where the pump curve meets the system curve.
Reciprocating pump flow is fixed by cylinder volume and speed; slip is the small difference between ideal and actual discharge.
Air vessels smooth the pulsating flow of a reciprocating pump and save part of the work lost to pipe friction.

glossary.def: A machine that adds energy to a liquid to move it from a lower level or pressure to a higher one.
A pump in which a rotating impeller continuously adds energy to flowing liquid.
A pump that traps a fixed volume of liquid and forces it into the delivery pipe.
The rotating wheel with vanes that transfers shaft work to the water in a centrifugal pump.
A spiral casing of increasing area around an impeller that slows the water and raises its pressure.
The pipe from the sump to the pump inlet, carrying water at pressure below atmospheric.
The pipe from the pump outlet to the destination.
Filling the pump casing and suction pipe with water before starting, to remove air.
The useful head developed by a pump, measured between suction and delivery gauge points.
The vertical height difference between the sump water level and the delivery level.
The head lost to friction in suction and delivery pipes and fittings.
The head equivalent to the kinetic energy of water, equal to V squared divided by 2g.
The ratio of manometric head to the head produced by the impeller.
The ratio of actual head developed to the ideal head from the impeller.
The ratio of power delivered to the water to the shaft power input.
The ratio of actual discharge to the discharge passing through the impeller, allowing for leakage.
The speed of a geometrically similar pump that would deliver unit discharge against unit head.
Net positive suction head: absolute pressure head at pump inlet minus vapour pressure head, in metres.
Boiling and collapse of liquid in low-pressure zones, causing erosion, noise and vibration.
The pressure at which a liquid boils at a given temperature.
The difference between ideal and actual discharge of a reciprocating pump, usually given as a percentage.
A closed chamber of compressed air connected to a pump pipe to smooth pulsating flow.
A pressure-volume diagram of the cylinder of a reciprocating pump.
The operating point where the pump characteristic curve meets the system curve.
A graph of the head required by a piping system against the discharge through it.
